title: The thousand years (Revelation 20)
hookLine: Christians read the millennium as literal, symbolic, or as the church age now
tomorrow: A new heaven and a new earth

cards: Three friends at a church potluck, paper plates in hand, get onto Revelation twenty. One says the thousand years are coming: Christ will return and reign on earth, a real, long age of peace.
The second says the gospel will slowly fill the world, and the long peace comes first, before he returns.

The third says it's happening already: the thousand years is a picture of now, the time of the church, with Christ reigning from heaven. All three have read the same chapter, and all three take it seriously.
And they go back for seconds together.

teach.b: Millennium means a thousand years, and the thousand years is this chapter's phrase. First, the text. An angel lays hold on "the dragon, that old serpent, which is the Devil, and Satan, and bound him a thousand years."
The faithful "lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years." Then the dragon is let loose for a little while, and finally defeated.
Second, the three readings. Some Christians, called premillennial, read a future reign of Christ on earth after he returns.
Some, called postmillennial, expect a long age of peace as the gospel spreads, and then his return.
And some, called amillennial, read the thousand years as symbolic: the present age of the church, with Christ reigning now. Augustine, in The City of God, read it that way.
Each reading has faithful Christians behind it, and churches have held them side by side. Third, a hint from another letter.

teach.h: A THOUSAND YEARS AS ONE DAY.
teach.b: Second Peter says: "one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day." Some readers take that as a caution against reading the number like a calendar. Fourth, what all three share.
However they read the thousand years, the chapter ends the same way: books are opened, the dead are judged by what they did, and "death and hell were cast into the lake of fire."
Death itself is thrown away. The friends argue over details; all three still say he reigns.

how: Churches and Christian teachers differ on the thousand years: some teach a future reign of Christ on earth, some a long age of peace before his return, and some read it as the present age of the church.

readers differ: a future reign, a long peace before his return, or the church age now.
Augustine read the thousand years as the present age of the church
in The City of God he read it symbolically, as the time of the church.
in Revelation 20 death survives to the end
"death and hell were cast into the lake of fire." death itself is thrown away.

games.q: you're at a church potluck. your friends are arguing about whether the thousand years are literal or symbolic. what does the chapter itself settle?
o: that the thousand years are exactly literal.
that the dragon is defeated and death is thrown away.
games.why: the text leaves room for the readings. what it ends on, for everyone, is the dragon defeated and death and hell cast into the lake of fire.

practice: Bring to mind a question about faith or life you don't have settled, maybe this one, maybe something closer to home.

Rest your hands open in your lap, as if holding it there: you don't have to drop it, and you don't have to grip it. If you pray, hold it up to God and say you'll trust what you can't yet see; if not, just breathe with an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Millennium. A thousand years, from Revelation twenty, read by Christians as a future reign, a coming age of peace, or the age of the church now.

orig.note: Greek: a thousand years, the phrase repeated through Revelation 20.

carryVoice: Your line: he reigns. Three readings of the thousand years, and one ending. Go gently.
